## T3 Code orchestration

The `t3-code` MCP server provides app-owned orchestration. Treat these concepts distinctly:

- A delegated task/subagent is child work owned by the current thread. Use `orchestrator_capabilities` to discover the current provider/model IDs from the same live catalog as the composer, including configured custom models. It lists a short set of models per provider; pass `search` to find others. Do not treat a native tool's model list as the full list of available subagent models. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use `delegate_task` with that provider instance and model when native tools cannot, including for same-provider work. Also use `delegate_task` for cross-provider or explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For a child task that needs a separate checkout, use `delegate_task` with `isolation:"worktree"` across any provider or model. It starts from the parent local commit and runs project setup; uncommitted edits are not copied. Retain each returned `taskId`, and use `task_status` or `task_cancel` to manage it.
- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` create ordinary top-level T3 conversations. Use them only when the user explicitly asks for separate/new/top-level threads or conversations. Never use them merely because the user said "subagent" or requested parallel delegated work.
- For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call `delegate_task` again. Include the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in each new task prompt. Track each round by its own `taskId`. Use a distinct `clientRequestId` per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use `t3_thread_send` on its `childThreadId`.

- `schedule_task` creates persistent recurring work in the app scheduler. Pass `schedule` as a structured object, never as JSON text: `{"type":"interval","everyMs":3600000}` for an interval, or `{"type":"fixed_time","timeOfDay":"09:00","weekdays":[1,2,3,4,5]}` for a wall-clock schedule, or `{"type":"webhook"}` to run on each request to the returned `webhookUrl` (the run sees the request only through `{{body.path}}`-style placeholders in the prompt). By default runs return to the current thread, which suits orchestrating: each trigger arrives here and you delegate or dedupe; set `bindToCurrentThread=false` only when the user wants a fresh thread for every run. After scheduling a timer, report the returned cadence and next run time; for a webhook, report its `webhookUrl`, or say T3 Connect remote access is needed if it is missing.
- When you need a secret from the user (a token, API key, or webhook signing secret), call `request_secret` so they enter it privately, then pass the returned `secretRef` to the tool that needs it, e.g. `signature.secretRef` on a webhook task for a sender that signs requests such as GitHub. A `secretRef` works once. Never ask for a secret in chat, never invent one, and never repeat one.
- To mention another thread to the user, link it as `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with its exact `threadId`, not URL-encoded. T3 Code opens the thread in the app and shows its current title.

### Choose the workspace before starting a new thread

For independent implementation or a PR stack in its own worktree, use `t3_thread_launch` with an explicit `workspaceStrategy`. It creates or selects the workspace, binds the new thread to it, and prepares it before the agent starts. Put the task in `message`, not `prompt`:

- New worktree: `{"title":"UI cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"worktree","baseRef":"feature/base","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup","startFromOrigin":false},"message":"Implement the cleanup and open a PR against feature/base."}`
- Existing worktree: `{"title":"Continue cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"existing_worktree","worktreePath":"/absolute/path/to/worktree","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup"},"message":"Continue the cleanup."}`
- Project's main checkout: `workspaceStrategy:{"type":"root"}`. Omitting workspaceStrategy also selects root; it does not inherit the caller's worktree.

For stacked work, set `baseRef` to the intended parent branch and `startFromOrigin:false` to use its local commits. Use `startFromOrigin:true` when you intend to fetch the base branch's remote and start from it. Uncommitted edits are not copied. Use `t3_worktree_list` to discover existing checkout paths. Project, model selection, and modes inherit unless supplied; a launched thread may not run with broader modes than yours.

`t3_thread_launch` is the single-thread launch tool. Use `create_threads` only for a batch of threads intentionally sharing the caller's checkout: it always inherits the caller's project, branch, and worktree and has no workspace override. Asking an agent to run `git worktree add` or `cd` in its prompt does not update T3's thread binding. Select the workspace in the launch call instead. `t3_worktree_handoff` moves the calling thread, not another thread, and cannot move a thread already attached to a worktree.

`t3_thread_launch` has no idempotency key. Retain its returned threadId and inspect it with `t3_thread_read` / `t3_thread_wait`; preparation can still be running after acceptance. If a launch fails or its response is lost, inspect `t3_thread_list` before retrying, since a thread may already exist.

Tool names may include a harness-normalized MCP prefix, such as `mcp__t3_code__delegate_task`; the semantics are the same. Some harnesses attach optional MCP servers lazily: if an initial tool-catalog scan does not show T3 tools, do not conclude that cross-provider delegation is unavailable. Make one bounded direct attempt using the known T3 tool name on the next tool step. In Codex code mode, for example, call `tools.mcp__t3_code__orchestrator_capabilities({})` before reporting that the capability is absent. Keep polling/wait loops bounded, do not duplicate active work, and use stable `clientRequestId` values when retrying tools that accept them.

ACP fallback: some ACP agents accept the injected MCP server but fail to expose its tools. When the T3 tools are absent and `T3_ACP_MCP_NODE` is present, call the same tools through the terminal: `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$T3_ACP_MCP_NODE" ${T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT:+"$T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT"} acp-mcp-call orchestrator_capabilities '{}'` (`T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT` is unset when T3 runs as a standalone executable). Delegate with `acp-mcp-call delegate_task '{"task":"...","target":{"providerInstanceId":"...","model":"..."},"mode":"async","clientRequestId":"..."}'`. This is the supported T3 transport fallback, not an ordinary shell-based substitute for delegation.

### Showing visuals

When a chart, table, diagram, image collage, or mockup would say more than prose, build a self-contained HTML page, check it with `html_preview`, then publish it with `html_render` before your final reply. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

- When model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty `inheritedOptions` from `orchestrator_capabilities`, use `delegate_task` even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Read the selected model's descriptors from `orchestrator_capabilities` and put settings in `target.options`, not only in the prompt. Claude commonly uses {"effort":"max","fastMode":true}; Codex uses {"reasoningEffort":"max","serviceTier":"priority"}. Do not translate max to high or ignore unsupported settings: report a capability mismatch. Options inherit only for the same provider instance and model; explicit entries override individual values, and [] or {} clears them. Check the returned providerInstanceId, model, and options against the requested selection.


### Background work you wait on

Before you end your turn to wait for a background command or Monitor you started, such as tests, a build, or a CI wait, call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID. The thread then stays in the user's Working list until that task ends, instead of returning to them early. Do not mark a dev server, a watcher, or anything else you leave running.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Preferences would hold the behavioral settings—language, appearance, AI providers, models, knowledge-base MCP servers, advanced options—keeping the two MCP concepts distinct since they're easily confused. My Desk itself would stay analytics-focused with just a small link pointing to the account's data section, using an all-time range there instead of the desk's scoped range.

name: twyne-browser-verification
description: "How to check twyne editor UI in a real browser here — headless Playwright env fix, free port, IndexedDB folio seeding, known flaky test pair"
metadata:

---

Recipe that worked on 2026-10-17 for verifying editor UI changes without the Convex backend:

- **Port:** 5173 may belong to another project (interleave-app). Start twyne with `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 bun run dev.frontend`.
- **Headless Playwright:** importing `node_modules/playwright/index.mjs` from a scratch script works, but Chromium fails to launch (GLIBC error from a nix alsa-lib) unless run as `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH node script.mjs`.
- **Skip onboarding:** a fresh profile redirects /editor/ to /dossier/create/. Instead, seed like `e2e/instruments.e2e.ts` `seed()`: route `/api/auth/` to `null`, visit a routed blank page, `import("/src/utils/idb.ts")` in page context, then call saveFoliosToIdb / saveFolioContentToIdb / saveActiveFolioIdToIdb (+ `signin-toast-dismissed` meta, `twyne:editor:view:v1` with zenMode false).
- **T3 preview tool:** its viewport can be zoomed or scaled (innerWidth ≠ the requested size), and evaluate/snapshot time out on heavy pages. Prefer the headless script for measurements.
- **Known flaky pair (pre-existing at HEAD bfa07af1):** `struggle-tracker.test.ts` and `quick-review.test.ts` fail together in one bun run (shared System One budget state). Each passes alone. Don't blame new changes for it.
- **Running e2e:** with the dev server on 5174, `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 npx playwright test <file>` works.
  - Screenshot suites (instruments, instrument-dock, instrument-room, living-desk) must run under `--config playwright.visual.config.ts`. It starts its own server on 5187 and compares against the committed `e2e/visual-baselines/`. The default config writes stray `e2e/*-snapshots/` folders; delete them afterwards.
  - About 38 default-config e2e tests already failed at HEAD bfa07af1 (checked on 2026-10-17 against a clean worktree). The causes:
    - The Pagination extension was unregistered in 0cb77885, so `__twynePagination` never appears. This breaks all of pagination and formatting, and most of drag-selection.
    - The "Go to page" combobox needs the Typst proof, which never typesets here. This breaks editor-declutter.
    - Tests expect a visible `.twyne-toolbar`, Bold, or read-aloud control, but zen is now the default and those sit in the collapsed Compositor. This breaks __responsive, select-all and read-aloud.
    - Tests expect a "File ▾" button and other masthead and drawer flows that have since changed. This breaks import and dossier-persistence.
  - Before blaming a change, run the same files against `git worktree add --detach /tmp/twyne-base HEAD` on port 5175 and diff the failing test names. The BYOK and drop-caret tests flake.
- **Qwik gotcha:** a component inside a closed `<details>` never runs its `useVisibleTask$` (it has no box). Mount it only while the disclosure is open.

Related: [[skip-long-verification]]

**Why:** On 2026-10-11 the user stopped a persona/voice redesign while it waited on the full suite and said "stop with the typechecking, move on without the tests."

**How to apply:** Run only the targeted test files for the code you changed, at most once, and only if they're quick. Never wait in a loop for long suites. In the summary, say which checks you skipped.

    - The Pagination extension was unregistered in 0cb77885, so `__twynePagination` never appears. This breaks all of pagination and formatting, and most of drag-selection.
    - The "Go to page" combobox needs the Typst proof, which never typesets here. This breaks editor-declutter.
    - Tests expect a visible `.twyne-toolbar`, Bold, or read-aloud control, but zen is now the default and those sit in the collapsed Compositor. This breaks __responsive, select-all and read-aloud.
    - Tests expect a "File ▾" button and other masthead and drawer flows that have since changed. This breaks import and dossier-persistence.

content.text:
I've reorganized account settings into three places, each with one job. I couldn't check the signed-in Account page in a browser, because that needs a real Not Organic sign-in.

| Page | What it's for | What's on it |
|---|---|---|
| **My Desk** `/desk/` | What you've done | Writing activity, AI usage, costs. The export/sync/delete block is replaced by a link to Account. |
| **Account** `/account/` (new) | Who you are and what you own | Twyne address (alias), public profile, what your profile shares, Not Organic, your data, CLI & MCP tokens, delete account. Links at the top jump to each section. |
| **Preferences** `/settings/` | How the app behaves | Language, appearance, about the writer, interview style, AI providers, models, research. Nothing account-related is left on it. |

**New features:**
- **Profile links:** you can add up to 6 links (website, Bluesky, newsletter…) on your profile. They show under your bio on your public page. Only `https` addresses are accepted, a bare `example.com` gets `https://` added, and a blank label falls back to the domain name.
- **Not Organic achievements:** the Account page shows the achievements you've earned across all Not Organic apps, read from Not Organic's own records. The same section shows your email, account ID (DID), and links to your wallet and Not Organic account.

**Other fixes:**
- Preferences was titled "The Editor's Desk", which was easy to confuse with My Desk. It's now "Preferences" in all six languages; I wrote the non-English versions myself, so a native speaker should check them.
- The account menu now reads My Desk → Account → Preferences.

**How it's built:** the profile, token and delete-account code moved out of the 5,500-line `settings/index.tsx` into `src/components/account/`, which takes that file down to about 4,100 lines. Profile links are a new optional `links` field on the `handles` table. Achievements come from a new action, `providerIdentity.getAchievements`.

**Checks:**
- Types check clean in the changed files.
- The targeted tests pass, including a new test for the profile-link rules. I updated the source-wiring tests for the new file locations.
- In a headless browser, `/account/`, `/settings/` and `/desk/` load with no page errors, but Account only showed its signed-out screen.
- I didn't run the full test suite or e2e tests.
- `convex codegen` contacted the dev deployment, but I didn't run `convex dev` or deploy.

**Before you rely on it:**
- **Usage export is now all-time.** On My Desk it exported the selected date range; on Account it exports your whole history.
- **There's still no whole-account export.** "Your data" covers usage history only, and each piece is still exported from its own folio menu. An "export everything" option would need a new backend job — tell me if you want it.
- **Achievements depend on Not Organic.** The Not Organic code allows Twyne to read them, but I haven't confirmed the live service accepts that from Twyne. If it doesn't, the section shows "could not be loaded" instead of breaking the page.

Nothing is committed yet.

Created 2026-10-23 at the user's request ("make a DID for this eval", cap $50):

- DID `did:plc:h7t2qykaxwf6s7iez6pmhs45`, handle `twyne-evals.pds.notorganic.info`, created on Not Organic's own PDS. It has signed in to the portal (id.notorganic.info) once, which makes it a known account there.
- skate: `twyne-eval-did` (the DID) and `twyne-evals-pds-password`. The account email is the user's Gmail plus-address `+twyne-evals`.
- **Session version 0.** The DID has no `didAccounts` row in Not Organic, so set `TWYNE_EVAL_SESSION_VERSION=0`. Without it, the gateway's `inference:begin` throws `session_revoked`, which the gateway does not map, so Twyne sees an opaque 500 `internal_error`.
- **Funding.** The first Twyne call auto-granted the $2.50 `twyne_welcome` lot; the portal's `/api/wallet` view doesn't show it. Any further credit needs an admin grant (Admin → Accounts → Direct grant, product scope Twyne); the cap the user set is $50 total. The production portal secret isn't reachable from this machine; no local notorganic-provider checkout links the prod Convex.
- **Reservations.** Each call reserves its alias ceiling up front (fast $0.25, balanced $0.50, reasoning $2.00), so parallel room calls need several dollars of headroom even though the actual cost is cents.
- **Signing config.** It comes from Twyne's *prod* Convex env: `npx convex env get --prod NOTORGANIC_ASSERTION_PRIVATE_KEY` (also `NOTORGANIC_ISSUER` and `NOTORGANIC_AUDIENCE`). The dev deployment has none.

**Gateway state as of 2026-10-23.** The running Not Organic gateway (Railway project `notorganic-provider`, service `gateway`, deployment 03c44bc7 from 2026-10-21) still holds revoked Keenable and TypeSafe keys. The working replacements are staged in its Railway variables (hash-matched against skate's `keenable-api-key@secrets` and `typesafe_api_key`) but not loaded. As a result `/v1/web/search` returns 502 and `/v1/judgement` returns 503 `judgement_invalid_configuration`. Production Twyne's editorial review gate and hosted claim checks are therefore silently off. Railway reports `canRedeploy: false`, so loading the keys needs a fresh build. The user chose not to deploy it on 2026-10-23.

**Eval workaround until that build ships:** `--system-one direct` (Jev with `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, honoured only by the loopback in-process app via `TWYNE_EVAL_JUDGEMENT_TRANSPORT`) and `--research keenable` (`evals/app/keenable-bridge.ts`, `KEENABLE_API_KEY`).

**Output ceiling.** The gateway's default output ceiling is around 4k tokens, and every text alias (fast/balanced/reasoning) routes to Inkling-Small, which can think past it. Twyne's `NO_OUTPUT_CEILING` is now 16,000 (convex/agents.ts).

Related: [[arize-workspace]], [[model-nicknames-for-delegation]].

**Live voice, 2026-10-28.** The gateway's `OPENAI_LIVE_API_KEY` returns 401 `invalid_api_key` from OpenAI. As a result, every Twyne Live session closes in under 1s, and the browser shows "Disconnected before final usage arrived". skate `openai-api-token@secrets` and `openai_api_key@secrets` both pass the `wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions` handshake; `openai-api@secrets` is also dead. The Bun relay (`apps/gateway/src/bun-realtime.ts`) logs nothing when the upstream fails. Fixed the same day: the key was set from `openai_api_key@secrets` and gateway deployment 2cf92906 succeeded. That deploy also loaded the Keenable/TypeSafe keys staged since 10-23, so the gateway-state note above may now be stale.

# Achievements and referrals: operator and integration guide

Status: implemented and tested locally. This work has not deployed code, created
promotions, issued rewards or changed live PDS records. A read-only production
check on 2026-10-10 found that hosted OAuth metadata still advertises only
`atproto`, and the gateway has no Baste or Frenzy assertion key configured.

## Enabling an integration

1. Keep each product's private Ed25519 assertion key in that product's backend.
   Configure only its public JWK on the gateway as
   `<PRODUCT>_ASSERTION_PUBLIC_JWK`. Key loading now uses `PRODUCT_IDS`, including
   Baste and Frenzy, and rejects private keys, wrong curves and invalid key use.
   The original four required keys remain required; missing optional products
   remain disabled without interrupting the others. Railway `preserve()` entries
   retain provisioned keys; they do not generate or install new credentials.
2. Deploy the Convex achievement/referral schema and functions before the
   gateway and portal that call them. Deploy the landing service's identity
   frontend as well: it serves the account UI on `id.notorganic.info`.
   The portal Dockerfile includes the shared `convex/publicProfile.ts` helper.
   The landing Dockerfile includes the portal's shared login, access and admin
   browser contracts. All three images build locally with the pinned Bun version.
3. Verify hosted client metadata advertises `transition:email`,
   `repo:info.notorganic.achievement` and `blob:image/png` in addition to
   `atproto`. Ordinary sign-in still requests only `atproto`; publishing is an
   explicit additional authorization. Deploying metadata alone grants no user
   permissions and does not upgrade existing sessions.
4. Run `rtk proxy bun scripts/check-account-integrations.ts --public-only` to
   check the hosted metadata. In an environment containing the gateway's public
   keys, omit `--public-only` and add `--require-product frenzy` (or `baste`) to
   check that integration. The command prints product names and validation
   failures, never key values. This narrow check does not establish a matching
   backend private key, deployed Convex functions or a real OAuth round trip.
5. Configure an achievement/referral policy below, then verify an authorized
   account flow, explicit publishing consent and public record/receipt before
   calling the integration live. Use zero rewards for non-promotional checks.

On 2026-10-10 Railway has no Frenzy service, and its Baste service has no
assertion-key variables. A backend destination is needed before those private
keys can be installed. Do not share another product's signing key to bypass this.

## Authority

- The Convex ledger (`convex/achievements.ts`, `convex/referrals.ts`) is the only
  authority for awards, claims and rewards. A PDS record (`info.notorganic.achievement`)
  is a display copy the owner can edit; never infer an award or reward from it.
- Writes come only from an application's server through the gateway with a
  service token. The DID is the token subject; the application is the token
  product. Request bodies never carry a DID.
- Credit is issued through the wallet grant path in the same transaction as the
  award or qualification, with deterministic keys (`achievement:<awardId>`,
  `referral:<claimId>:referrer|referee`). Retries replay; they never pay twice.

## Setting up (administrators)

Portal → Admin → **Achievements and referrals**. The panel only renders for
accounts with admin access. The portal checks session, CSRF and admin access on
`/api/admin/*`; Convex re-checks the `NOTORGANIC_ADMIN_DIDS` allowlist and writes
every change to the admin audit log.

- **Achievement**: application, key (`first-lesson`), title, description, image
  path (a PNG under `/achievements/` or `/brand/` served by the portal), optional
  credit. Credit is blank (zero) by default. Only set it for an approved promotion.
  Turning an achievement off stops new awards; already-issued awards keep the
  title, description and image they were issued with.
- **Referral policy**: application, the event name the application will report
  (for example `first_purchase`), referrer and new-member credit (both zero by
  default). Without an active policy, no referral qualifies or pays.

API equivalents: `GET|PUT /api/admin/achievements`, `PUT /api/admin/referral-policies`.

### Starter catalog

`unison/src/achievement-catalog.u` defines 48 starter achievements, six for each
registered application (Not Organic, Keating, Twyne, Interleave, Stich, Voxq,
Baste, Frenzy). On the native account pages, **Admin → Starter catalog → Install**
adds every entry that is missing. Each one goes through the same audited
`PUT /api/admin/achievements` route as a hand edit, with zero credit. Entries that
already exist, including ones an operator changed, are skipped. If a definition
is refused, installation stops there; running it again continues from that point.

Installing a definition only makes it awardable. Nothing is awarded until an
application's backend calls `POST /v1/achievements/awards` with that key. Wiring
those calls into each product is still to do.

Tier (Seed, Sprout, Bloom, Evergreen), points, growth levels, hints and hidden
achievements are presentation only. They come from the catalog module, never
enter the ledger, and award no credit. A hidden achievement shows its hint until
it is earned. Badge art lives at `apps/portal/public/achievements/<app>/<key>.png`
and is generated by `rtk proxy bun scripts/achievement-art.ts` (needs ImageMagick
with librsvg). Regenerate it after adding catalog entries.

### Celebrations

When the account pages show an award this browser has not celebrated yet, they
play an unlock animation: the badge spins in with a WebGL foil, each
application has its own background shader, and points count up. Awards from the
last 21 days are celebrated; older ones are marked as seen without one, so a new
device does not replay a whole history. Seen award IDs are kept in this
browser's `localStorage` and nowhere else. With reduced motion, the card still
appears but nothing moves, and no WebGL runs. Without JavaScript, nothing is
celebrated, and the collection, filters and every action still work.

## Rules the ledger enforces

Achievements
- An application issues only its own achievements. Inactive definitions cannot be
  awarded, but a retry of an award that already succeeded replays.
- No award to a deleted account (account `deletedAt` or a provider deletion
  request), a locked/recovering account, or a suspended/deleted app mapping.

Referrals
- A click on `/r/<code>` only redirects with `?ref=<code>`; it records nothing.
- A claim is recorded by the application's server after sign-in. Rejected: self
  referral, a second referrer for the same account and app, accounts that joined
  the app before the code existed, revoked codes, codes whose owner is deleted or
  inactive.
- Frenzy may record claims for other applications (cross-app viral loops), but
  its assertion does not prove membership in the target app, so the referee must
  already have an active mapping for that app.

I'm sketching the achievements design: an internal `awardAchievement` action in Twyne's backend that resolves the DID and calls the ledger's awards endpoint using the achievements:award capability, with idempotency handled both server-side and via a local tracking table to prevent duplicate sends. Now I'm thinking through which triggers should fire these awards.

Since Twyne is local-first with manuscripts stored in IndexedDB, I need to figure out what server-visible signals exist for each achievement — things like first manuscript creation, word count milestones, publishing events, citation counts, and other client-side detections like notes or revision tracking. Given memory limits on actions, I'm considering splitting each table's data into NDJSON chunk blobs stored separately, with the job recording chunk ids so the client can later assemble a manifest plus chunks into a zip -- I should check whether a zip library like jszip or fflate is already a dependency. I'm also weighing whether to include associated storage blobs like images or avatars in the export.

For the manifest, I'll fetch storage URLs for binary files and bundle them into the zip rather than linking externally, while excluding sensitive fields like integration token hashes, rate buckets, and presence data. I should also schedule cleanup of export storage files after 24 hours, and check whether an existing backup/export helper already handles local IDB folio data before building a new one.

content.thinking:
I'm identifying citations by counting endnote/footnote markers per folio, treating ten or more as well-sourced. Now I'm sketching the schema for an achievementGrants table tracking ownership, status, and attempts, and planning the achievements module with an internal query to evaluate progress.

For evaluation, I'm leaning toward an internalAction that pulls criteria snapshots across folios, published status, and accepted suggestions, using paginated scans since suggestion counts could be large. I'm considering a helper internal query that scans a page of rows and returns derived facts like word/citation counts and acceptance flags, which the action then aggregates before awarding any newly earned achievements and recording them in the grants table. For the public-facing refresh mutation, I'm thinking through how to rate-limit it per user, possibly by storing a lastCheckedAt timestamp somewhere accessible.

I'm settling on a single-row-per-user `achievementState` table storing ownerId, checkedAt, and awarded achievement IDs, where the mutation no-ops if checked within the last ten minutes and otherwise updates checkedAt and schedules the evaluation action. I'd hook this into the publish flow via a shared `scheduleAchievementCheck` helper that fires unconditionally since the check itself is cheap. On the client side, I'm working out whether getAchievements should itself trigger evaluation before listing, so newly earned achievements show immediately without a race between the refresh mutation and the list fetch, while also considering how to award achievements autonomously even if the user never visits the Account page.

Now I'm thinking the autonomous trigger should come from the periodic sync push mutation — I'll have it call `scheduleAchievementCheck` with the user's DID-linked subject, respecting the cooldown so it only writes when the cooldown has elapsed, avoiding OCC contention on every sync. The publish hook would force an evaluation regardless of cooldown. The evaluation action needs to resolve the subject via providerIdentities, and awarding should track already-granted keys in the state row, skipping those and retrying unawarded ones (e.g. if a definition isn't installed yet, returning 404) on the next check. content.content:
## Setting up (administrators)

Portal → Admin → **Achievements and referrals**. The panel only renders for
accounts with admin access. The portal checks session, CSRF and admin access on
`/api/admin/*`; Convex re-checks the `NOTORGANIC_ADMIN_DIDS` allowlist and writes
every change to the admin audit log.

- **Achievement**: application, key (`first-lesson`), title, description, image
  path (a PNG under `/achievements/` or `/brand/` served by the portal), optional
  credit. Credit is blank (zero) by default. Only set it for an approved promotion.
  Turning an achievement off stops new awards; already-issued awards keep the
  title, description and image they were issued with.
- **Referral policy**: application, the event name the application will report
  (for example `first_purchase`), referrer and new-member credit (both zero by
  default). Without an active policy, no referral qualifies or pays.

API equivalents: `GET|PUT /api/admin/achievements`, `PUT /api/admin/referral-policies`.

### Starter catalog

`unison/src/achievement-catalog.u` defines 48 starter achievements, six for each
registered application (Not Organic, Keating, Twyne, Interleave, Stich, Voxq,
Baste, Frenzy). On the native account pages, **Admin → Starter catalog → Install**
adds every entry that is missing. Each one goes through the same audited
`PUT /api/admin/achievements` route as a hand edit, with zero credit. Entries that
already exist, including ones an operator changed, are skipped. If a definition
is refused, installation stops there; running it again continues from that point.

Installing a definition only makes it awardable. Nothing is awarded until an
application's backend calls `POST /v1/achievements/awards` with that key. Wiring
those calls into each product is still to do.

content.text:
Export everything is built and its tests pass. Achievement code is done in Twyne too, but no awards will go through until someone with admin access installs Twyne's achievements on Not Organic. Its ledger currently rejects them with "achievement not defined for this application".

**To turn achievements on:** sign in to id.notorganic.info with an admin account and click **Admin → Starter catalog → Install**. I couldn't do this without an admin session. It's a one-click step that adds the six Twyne achievements at zero credit. Their keys and wording match what Twyne now checks for.

**Export everything** (Account → Your data):
- Clicking it starts a background job on the server. It packs every synced row you own into a zip, along with your files: images, profile picture and manuscript version history (`.lix`). Your Not Organic achievements are included too. The job runs in `convex/accountExport.ts` and `convex/accountExportBuild.ts`.
- When you download it, the browser adds a `this-device/` folder. That folder holds the folios, manuscripts, briefs, personas, comments, settings and usage history kept only on that device.
- API keys and token secrets are never included, and other accounts' rows never appear.
- The zip is kept for 24 hours, then deleted. Deleting your account also deletes any exports.
- I added `fflate` as a dependency to build the zip.

**Achievements:**
- About a minute after you sync, accept an edit or publish, the server checks your synced data. It then awards anything you've newly earned on the Not Organic ledger, each one only once. Opening the Account page also runs a check and shows everything you've earned across all Not Organic apps.
- What earns each one:
  - **First draft:** any manuscript.
  - **Notes from the room:** you accept a persona's edit.
  - **Kill your darlings:** you accept an edit that deletes a passage.
  - **Well sourced:** 10 footnotes or endnotes in one manuscript.
  - **Ten thousand words:** 10,000 words across your manuscripts.
  - **Out the door:** you publish a piece. Exporting a piece doesn't count yet, though the catalog says "publish or export".
- Accounts that aren't linked to Not Organic are never sent an award.

**Live checks against Not Organic:**
- Twyne can read achievements: the dedicated `twyne-evals` test account returned an empty list.
- Twyne's sign-in for awarding is accepted. A request with a made-up achievement was turned away without writing anything.
- To check one real achievement, I tried to award `first-draft` to `twyne-evals`. It was rejected because it isn't defined yet, which is the blocker above.

**Tests:**
- New tests cover the export job (only your own rows, no token secret, files intact, deleted after expiry). The award tests use a stand-in for Not Organic and check that the right achievements are sent once and that unlinked accounts get nothing.
- Those passed, as did the existing account, profile, Typst sync and page-wiring tests.
- The Convex code and the new frontend files typecheck clean. The full `tsc` run times out here, so I checked only the changed files, and I didn't run the full suite.

`convex codegen` pushed this code to your Convex dev deployment, not production. Nothing is committed yet.

content.content:
# Deploying Twyne

Twyne ships as a Qwik City SSR app. The browser bundle is built by Vite into
`dist/`, the SSR server entry into `server/`, and `server.js` (Node `http`)
serves both and listens on `$PORT`.

## Railway (primary)

The repo is configured for [Railway](https://railway.com) via `railway.json`
(`builder: RAILPACK`) and [`railpack.json`](https://railpack.com) — Railpack is
Railway's successor to Nixpacks:

- **Install** (Bun): `bun install --frozen-lockfile`
- **Build** (Bun): `bash scripts/railway-build.sh` — runs Convex deploy + Vite
  client + Vite SSR server. If `CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY` is unset, the script
  degrades to a frontend-only build (backend left untouched).
- **Start** (Node): `node server.js`
- **Healthcheck**: `GET /`

> The `build` step is auto-generated by Railpack from the Node provider
> (uses the mise step to install `bun` + `node`, then runs
> `bun install --frozen-lockfile`). We only override the `build` step to
> inject the Convex deploy + Vite build via `scripts/railway-build.sh` —
> the script is required because the inline `if/then/else` with nested
> single-quoted `&&` strings gets mangled by the build step's shell
> serialization.

`railpack.json` pins `node: 20` + `bun: 1` so the runtime image has `node`
available for the start command (`server.js` uses `node:http`), while Bun does
the install and Vite build.

### One-time setup

1. **Create / link the service** (already linked to `Diogenesoftoronto/twyne`):

   ```bash
   railway add --service twyne --repo Diogenesoftoronto/twyne
   ```

   Railway auto-deploys on every push to the connected branch.

2. **Set environment variables** (see `.env.example` for the full list). The
   `VITE_*` values are baked in at build time, so they must be set on the
   service before the first build:

{
  "$schema": "https://railway.com/railway.schema.json",
  "build": {
    "builder": "RAILPACK"
  },
  "deploy": {
    "startCommand": "node server.js",
    "healthcheckPath": "/",
    "healthcheckTimeout": 120,
    "restartPolicyType": "ON_FAILURE",
    "restartPolicyMaxRetries": 5
  }
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Railway build step: deploy Convex backend (when key is configured), then
# build the Qwik City frontend + SSR server.
#
# Gating: when CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY is unset (frontend-only deploys, preview
# environments, local re-runs) we still build the frontend but skip the
# backend push.

set -euo pipefail

if [ -n "${CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY:-}" ]; then
  echo "==> Deploying Convex backend"
  # 1.46 fixes index-removal review with deploy-only keys. Keep CI deployment
  # tooling explicit even when the app's lockfile pins an older client.
  npx --yes convex@1.46.0 deploy --cmd 'bun run build.client && bun run build.server'
else
  echo "==> CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY not set — building frontend only, skipping convex deploy"
  bun run build.client
  bun run build.server
fi

I fixed the sign-in panel in the account menu and deployed it. In the signed-out menu, the sign-in text and the "Continue with Not Organic" button label now wrap inside the panel instead of running past its edge. **Fix:** a one-line change to the dropdown in `src/components/auth/account-menu.tsx`. It now allows wrapping itself, so it renders correctly anywhere it's placed. I also capped its width so it can't be wider than a narrow screen.

**Check:** I opened the signed-out editor in a headless browser with the menu open, at desktop width and at 390px phone width. Nothing overflows at either size, and on the phone the heading and button label each wrap to two lines.

The same edit is also uncommitted in your `feat/clairic-extraction` working tree, matching what's on `main`.

+> **Implementation note (2026-10-21).** The shipped bench was narrowed to **Compare a revision**: the writer selects one sentence, edits one copy, reads the word diff in the paragraph, and may explicitly ask the configured prose model to read the difference (at most two observations, each quoting the original, the revision and any paragraph text it relies on; quotes are validated in code and the reading is discarded when any of those texts change). Rewrite candidates, rule rewrites, Words, Place, Compare, meaning probabilities and automatic opening were removed from this surface. It works with no sentence history. This is a focused hypothesis — that a reading of the writer's own revision surfaces consequences they had not noticed — not validated demand; if readings are usually obvious or absent, the bench should be retired rather than widened. The design below is kept as the original proposal.

content.text:
I committed everything and pushed it to `feat/clairic-extraction`, not to `main`. Pushing to `main` deploys to production, so that's a separate yes from you.

First I fast-forwarded the branch to `main` (it was 15 commits behind), then replayed your uncommitted work on top. That gave 14 conflicting files and 25 files that clashed with untracked copies. Most were the same fixes you'd already committed to `main` since Oct 20, so I kept `main`'s committed version for those.

Where both sides held real changes, I chose:
- **Quote links:** I kept your uncommitted stricter rule over `main`'s Oct 20 "closest passage" links. A near match now shows as an unlinked "possible related passage", never as a quote link.
- **Eval harness:** 7 eval files had edits from Oct 24, after `main`'s commit, so I kept those. That means the older inline Clairic date-uncertainty test is gone; the new value-support tests cover it.

**New commits:**
1. Upgrade Qwik to `2.0.0-rc.4` (from the 2.0 betas).
2. Never show a paraphrase as an exact quotation, plus the persona panel and comment styles that go with it.
3. Ignore a credit-runway forecast that arrives after you've moved on.
4. Score focus forecasts against the outcome they actually predict.
5. Narrow the Sentence bench to "Compare a revision", with docs, manual and e2e updates.
6. Score research sources on Clairic value support (eval harness).
7. Add the comments design study, the UX brief and the `tools/flint-traces` model explorer.

**Checks:**
- The production build succeeds with the Qwik upgrade.
- The eval harness passes (65 tests), as do the targeted Convex tests and the changed unit test files when run one at a time.
- Some test files fail when run in one batch because their mocks leak into each other; I didn't fix that.
- I didn't run e2e tests or the full suite. The Sentence bench commit includes updated screenshot baselines that I didn't regenerate.

**Left out or changed:**
- The design study's 20 MB zip duplicated its loose PNGs, so I moved it to `/tmp/twyne-wt-backup/` and updated its README and checksums.
- A copy of the UX brief at the repo root was identical to the one in `docs/`, so I deleted it.
- I added `__pycache__/` to `.gitignore`.

**Safety copies:** your pre-merge work is still in `git stash` (`stash@{0}`, "wt-before-ff-main"), and as a patch plus tarball in `/tmp/twyne-wt-backup/`. Drop them once you're happy.

## T3 Code orchestration

The `t3-code` MCP server provides app-owned orchestration. Treat these concepts distinctly:

- A delegated task/subagent is child work owned by the current thread. Use `orchestrator_capabilities` to discover the current provider/model IDs from the same live catalog as the composer, including configured custom models. It lists a short set of models per provider; pass `search` to find others. Do not treat a native tool's model list as the full list of available subagent models. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use `delegate_task` with that provider instance and model when native tools cannot, including for same-provider work. Also use `delegate_task` for cross-provider or explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For a child task that needs a separate checkout, use `delegate_task` with `isolation:"worktree"` across any provider or model. It starts from the parent local commit and runs project setup; uncommitted edits are not copied. Retain each returned `taskId`, and use `task_status` or `task_cancel` to manage it.
- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` create ordinary top-level T3 conversations. Use them only when the user explicitly asks for separate/new/top-level threads or conversations. Never use them merely because the user said "subagent" or requested parallel delegated work.
- For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call `delegate_task` again. Include the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in each new task prompt. Track each round by its own `taskId`. Use a distinct `clientRequestId` per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use `t3_thread_send` on its `childThreadId`.

- `schedule_task` creates persistent recurring work in the app scheduler. Pass `schedule` as a structured object, never as JSON text: `{"type":"interval","everyMs":3600000}` for an interval, or `{"type":"fixed_time","timeOfDay":"09:00","weekdays":[1,2,3,4,5]}` for a wall-clock schedule, or `{"type":"webhook"}` to run on each request to the returned `webhookUrl` (the run sees the request only through `{{body.path}}`-style placeholders in the prompt). By default runs return to the current thread, which suits orchestrating: each trigger arrives here and you delegate or dedupe; set `bindToCurrentThread=false` only when the user wants a fresh thread for every run. After scheduling a timer, report the returned cadence and next run time; for a webhook, report its `webhookUrl`, or say T3 Connect remote access is needed if it is missing.
- When you need a secret from the user (a token, API key, or webhook signing secret), call `request_secret` so they enter it privately, then pass the returned `secretRef` to the tool that needs it, e.g. `signature.secretRef` on a webhook task for a sender that signs requests such as GitHub. A `secretRef` works once. Never ask for a secret in chat, never invent one, and never repeat one.
- To mention another thread to the user, link it as `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with its exact `threadId`, not URL-encoded. T3 Code opens the thread in the app and shows its current title.

### Choose the workspace before starting a new thread

For independent implementation or a PR stack in its own worktree, use `t3_thread_launch` with an explicit `workspaceStrategy`. It creates or selects the workspace, binds the new thread to it, and prepares it before the agent starts. Put the task in `message`, not `prompt`:

- New worktree: `{"title":"UI cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"worktree","baseRef":"feature/base","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup","startFromOrigin":false},"message":"Implement the cleanup and open a PR against feature/base."}`
- Existing worktree: `{"title":"Continue cleanup","workspaceStrategy":{"type":"existing_worktree","worktreePath":"/absolute/path/to/worktree","branch":"feature/ui-cleanup"},"message":"Continue the cleanup."}`
- Project's main checkout: `workspaceStrategy:{"type":"root"}`. Omitting workspaceStrategy also selects root; it does not inherit the caller's worktree.

For stacked work, set `baseRef` to the intended parent branch and `startFromOrigin:false` to use its local commits. Use `startFromOrigin:true` when you intend to fetch the base branch's remote and start from it. Uncommitted edits are not copied. Use `t3_worktree_list` to discover existing checkout paths. Project, model selection, and modes inherit unless supplied; a launched thread may not run with broader modes than yours.

`t3_thread_launch` is the single-thread launch tool. Use `create_threads` only for a batch of threads intentionally sharing the caller's checkout: it always inherits the caller's project, branch, and worktree and has no workspace override. Asking an agent to run `git worktree add` or `cd` in its prompt does not update T3's thread binding. Select the workspace in the launch call instead. `t3_worktree_handoff` moves the calling thread, not another thread, and cannot move a thread already attached to a worktree.

`t3_thread_launch` has no idempotency key. Retain its returned threadId and inspect it with `t3_thread_read` / `t3_thread_wait`; preparation can still be running after acceptance. If a launch fails or its response is lost, inspect `t3_thread_list` before retrying, since a thread may already exist.

Tool names may include a harness-normalized MCP prefix, such as `mcp__t3_code__delegate_task`; the semantics are the same. Some harnesses attach optional MCP servers lazily: if an initial tool-catalog scan does not show T3 tools, do not conclude that cross-provider delegation is unavailable. Make one bounded direct attempt using the known T3 tool name on the next tool step. In Codex code mode, for example, call `tools.mcp__t3_code__orchestrator_capabilities({})` before reporting that the capability is absent. Keep polling/wait loops bounded, do not duplicate active work, and use stable `clientRequestId` values when retrying tools that accept them.

ACP fallback: some ACP agents accept the injected MCP server but fail to expose its tools. When the T3 tools are absent and `T3_ACP_MCP_NODE` is present, call the same tools through the terminal: `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$T3_ACP_MCP_NODE" ${T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT:+"$T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT"} acp-mcp-call orchestrator_capabilities '{}'` (`T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT` is unset when T3 runs as a standalone executable). Delegate with `acp-mcp-call delegate_task '{"task":"...","target":{"providerInstanceId":"...","model":"..."},"mode":"async","clientRequestId":"..."}'`. This is the supported T3 transport fallback, not an ordinary shell-based substitute for delegation.

### Showing visuals

When a chart, table, diagram, image collage, or mockup would say more than prose, build a self-contained HTML page, check it with `html_preview`, then publish it with `html_render` before your final reply. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

- When model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty `inheritedOptions` from `orchestrator_capabilities`, use `delegate_task` even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Read the selected model's descriptors from `orchestrator_capabilities` and put settings in `target.options`, not only in the prompt. Claude commonly uses {"effort":"max","fastMode":true}; Codex uses {"reasoningEffort":"max","serviceTier":"priority"}. Do not translate max to high or ignore unsupported settings: report a capability mismatch. Options inherit only for the same provider instance and model; explicit entries override individual values, and [] or {} clears them. Check the returned providerInstanceId, model, and options against the requested selection.


### Background work you wait on

Before you end your turn to wait for a background command or Monitor you started, such as tests, a build, or a CI wait, call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID. The thread then stays in the user's Working list until that task ends, instead of returning to them early. Do not mark a dev server, a watcher, or anything else you leave running.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"
