tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_list
tools.description: List T3 threads in a project, newest first. Omit projectId for the calling thread's project. Filter by durable run status, title, or settled state (settled=true lists threads the user or auto-settlement moved out of the active list), or snoozed state, and paginate with the returned cursor. A snoozed thread wakes early only when it asks for something or fails after snoozing; completed runs and background wakes keep it snoozed. pullRequests lists every pull request linked to each thread; linkedPullRequest is a legacy single link and can be null while pullRequests still has entries. To link a thread for the user, write `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with the threadId exactly as returned, not URL-encoded; T3 Code shows the thread's current title.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_read
tools.description: Read durable state and a paginated timeline from any T3 thread in this environment. The default messages view returns user messages, assistant messages, and proposed plans; activity returns all summarized timeline items. Reading an untruncated terminal assistant result from this parent thread's direct app-owned child acknowledges that child's automatic completion delivery. Continue with afterPosition=nextPosition. Recover long item text with itemId and textOffset=nextTextOffset until nextTextOffset is null; offsets count UTF-16 code units. The thread also reports its snooze state and, in pullRequests, every linked pull request; linkedPullRequest is a legacy single link and can be null while pullRequests still has entries. To link a thread for the user, write `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with the threadId exactly as returned, not URL-encoded; T3 Code shows the thread's current title.

limit.description: Maximum timeline items to return, from 1 to 100.

runLimit.description: Maximum recent runs to return, from 1 to 50.

maxCharsPerItem.description: Maximum text characters per item, from 1 to 50000.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_search
tools.description: Search active threads the way the command palette does: title, branch, pull request, and project matches first (source "title", ranked by match quality and recent use, with one-typo tolerance), then threads whose messages contain every query word of three or more characters (source "user" or "assistant", with a snippet; up to a fifth of the limit is kept for these). Subagent threads are skipped. Limited to one project (projectId, else the calling thread's project); a caller outside a T3 thread that omits projectId searches every project. No pagination or exhaustive-result guarantee.

The Not Organic gateway's OpenAI key for Live voice is dead, so voice can't start for any account, not just yours. "Disconnected before final usage arrived" is a misleading catch-all the browser shows whenever the socket closes without a proper end-of-session message (`src/utils/live-voice.ts:554`).

**What happens on each attempt:**
1. Twyne's checks all pass. The Railway logs at 08:18 UTC today show `/v1/wallet` 200, `/v1/realtime/consent` 200 and the token exchange 200, so your credit, consent and sign-in are fine.
2. The gateway accepts the Live connection and then tries to open its own connection to OpenAI with `OPENAI_LIVE_API_KEY`.
3. OpenAI rejects that key with **401 `invalid_api_key`**. I confirmed this by testing the gateway's key directly against `wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions`.
4. The gateway's relay (`apps/gateway/src/bun-realtime.ts`) closes the connection without sending an error message, and it logs nothing. Twyne's relay just passes the close through, so the browser lands in its generic "closed early" message.

Both of your attempts at 08:18 closed within half a second. There hasn't been a successful Live session in the last 7 days.

**You weren't charged.** OpenAI never accepted the connection, so the gateway took the "never started" path (`live_not_started`) and released the $0.50 hold.

## Fix

Replace `OPENAI_LIVE_API_KEY` on the `notorganic-provider` → `gateway` Railway service, then redeploy. Both of your attempts at 08:18 closed within half a second. There hasn't been a successful Live session in the last 7 days.

**You weren't charged.** OpenAI never accepted the connection, so the gateway took the "never started" path (`live_not_started`) and released the $0.50 hold.

## Why voice fails

The Not Organic gateway's OpenAI key for Live voice is dead, so voice can't start for any account, not just yours. "Disconnected before final usage arrived" is a misleading catch-all the browser shows whenever the socket closes without a proper end-of-session message (`src/utils/live-voice.ts:554`).

**What happens on each attempt:**
1. Twyne's checks all pass. The Railway logs at 08:18 UTC today show `/v1/wallet` 200, `/v1/realtime/consent` 200 and the token exchange 200, so your credit, consent and sign-in are fine.
2. The gateway accepts the Live connection and then tries to open its own connection to OpenAI with `OPENAI_LIVE_API_KEY`.
3. OpenAI rejects that key with **401 `invalid_api_key`**. I confirmed this by testing the gateway's key directly against `wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions`.
4. The gateway's relay (`apps/gateway/src/bun-realtime.ts`) closes the connection without sending an error message, and it logs nothing. Twyne's relay just passes the close through, so the browser lands in its generic "closed early" message.

Both of your attempts at 08:18 closed within half a second. There hasn't been a successful Live session in the last 7 days.

**You weren't charged.** OpenAI never accepted the connection, so the gateway took the "never started" path (`live_not_started`) and released the $0.50 hold.

## Fix

Replace `OPENAI_LIVE_API_KEY` on the `notorganic-provider` → `gateway` Railway service, then redeploy. Last time Railway reported `canR

- **Size:** Supertonic is about 260 MB (the files listed in `browser-inference.ts`) and already runs in the browser with WebGPU, falling back to WASM. LFM3 audio is about 2.2B parameters, roughly 1.5 GB or more even compressed, and I found no browser runtime for it yet.
- **Narration:** reading a chapter aloud doesn't need conversation, just good, consistent voices. Supertonic's fixed voice embeddings are made for exactly that. I haven't seen anything on LFM3's voice quality, its voice choices, or how it holds up over long passages.

**My suggestion:**
- Use LFM3 audio for local Live: desktop first, and as the fallback when credits run out.
- Keep Supertonic for in-browser narration until a side-by-side test says otherwise. I can add that test to the L

The 10-22 commit is just a checkpoint branch, so the real port state is HEAD, last touched 10-12. Next I'm reading the native AI and audio foundations to pick the slice to mount.

I've identified the gap: the local-model process manager in the native AI layer is a stub that always reports "unavailable." I'll implement real launch, readiness-check, and shutdown logic modeled on `desktop/litert-server.ts`, starting by reading that reference file.
use terra swarms to implement things quickly
Terra is `codex` / `gpt-6.1-terra`. Before splitting the work into lanes with no overlapping files, I'm checking the audio module and how the build is set up.

Disk usage is at 93% with no build cache yet, so I'll run Terra lanes from a single checkout with disjoint file ownership and a shared cargo target rather than separate worktrees. Now checking which modules build without GPUI.
I'm planning three isolated Terra worktree lanes covering LiteRT lifecycle, HTTP/SSE transport, and native audio—first checking which options Terra accepts.
I'm dividing the work into three isolated Terra worktree lanes, and starting by locating the web app's provider settings so I can reference them in the lane briefs.
Starting the three Terra lanes now.
All three Terra lanes are running. I'm adding "Terra" to the model nicknames note so the shorthand works next time.

Three Terra workers are now building parts of the desktop port in parallel. Each has its own worktree, so they don't touch your dirty `feat/clairic-extraction` checkout or each other's files.

**Where the port stood:** the last real work was on 10-12. The editor, Typst, Dossier, Board panels and Appearance settings are well along. The AI, audio and connected-account pieces exist as tested types and logic, but none of them can actually do anything yet. Every live path deliberately reports "unavailable". These three lanes make the first of those real:

| Lane | What becomes real |
|---|---|
| **A: Local AI** | Starting and stopping the local LiteRT model (ported from `desktop/litert-server.ts`), and real streaming requests to local model servers (LiteRT, Ollama, OpenAI-compatible) |
| **B: Audio devices** | Real speaker playback and microphone capture with `cpal`, which Narration and Live voice both need; also adds `alsa-lib` to `devenv.nix` |
| **C: AI settings** | A native AI providers section in Settings, under Appearance: add, edit, remove and choose providers, saved in a format the web app can read |

Each worker runs only its own module's tests and Clippy, then commits to its branch. When they report back, I'll merge the three branches, check the combined build, and update `PORT_PLAN.md`.

The next step after that is a native Live voice desk on top of A and B. That's also where the local LFM3 audio model would plug in as the offline/no-credit fallback.

I've added "Terra"

Lane A stopped without implementing anything: it abandoned an unvalidated draft and killed its compile partway through. Its thread already has the code context, so I'm sending it back to finish rather than starting over.

Lane A (local AI) came back with nothing done. Its draft of the LiteRT start/stop code didn't meet the cancellation and process-cleanup requirements yet, so it threw the draft away. It also stopped its test build partway through. No code was committed and no tests ran.

3. **Let the first build finish** instead of stopping it.
4. **If start/stop stalls, commit the transport anyway** and report what's left.

Lanes B (audio devices) and C (AI settings) are still running. Once all three report back, I'll merge them and check the combined build.

content.content:
=== 569b7d17
Upload persona notes filed by an old pull
Before July a pull filed notes and replies in the server's shape:
createdAt where the app keeps timestamp, replyId where it keeps id. A
device that signed in then still holds them, and pushed them without the
createdAt the server requires. The server refused every such push, and
the folios and drafts in it went with it, so that writing never reached
the account or any other device.

The local loaders now read either shape, which also gives those notes
their real age in the margin.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>


 src/utils/convex-sync.test.ts | 48 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/utils/convex-sync.ts      | 39 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++--------
 2 files changed, 79 insertions(+), 8 deletions(-)
=== 90dbdedc
Let the editor reach the shared document relay
The relay lives on the Convex site origin and the editor on twyne.love.
Its JSON body and session header make the browser ask permission first,
and the relay never answered, so every get, pull and push failed with
"Failed to fetch" before it was sent. No shared folio could be opened
or kept in sync.

The relay now answers that check for Twyne's own origins, reusing the
list sign-in trusts, and marks its replies readable by them. Other
origins are refused. The session interceptor also kept only the headers
it added, dropping the SDK's Content-Type; it now keeps the request's own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

 5 files changed, 184 insertions(+), 10 deletions(-)
=== c09daa9d
Install the shared document session header when the page is ready
The root component's first element is <head>, which is never on screen,
so its visible task never ran. The Lix relay fetch wrapper therefore was
never installed, and every shared document request went out without the
session. Running the task when the document is ready installs it on
every page, and lets the System theme follow the OS as intended.

content.thinking:
I'm realizing there's a real problem: every remote-sync event remounts the editor by bumping the folio key and reloading, which re-seeds it entirely. This only fires when the remote revision exceeds the local one and nothing's dirty or pushing, but I'm worried about a race where a subscription update arrives before the push mutation's result comes back, which could cause an unwanted remount right after our own edit.

I'm checking whether Convex guarantees that mutation results resolve only after queries reflect the new state, which would mean onUpdate fires while pushing is still true and safely bails out. More concerning is that pullAll sends the entire account snapshot — every manuscript's HTML and Typst content — on every push, and the client parses that whole payload every few seconds while typing, which could easily block the main thread for larger accounts.

Better approach: subscribe to a lightweight sync-revision query and only fetch the full pullAll payload when the revision advances past what's known locally, since the tab that pushed already knows its own revision and skips the fetch. This cuts bandwidth to one fetch per change for tabs that actually need it, though frequent edits (e.g. pushing every 4s) could still make an open tab B fetch repeatedly, so coalescing revision changes with a short wait might help.

For hidden tabs I'm considering deferring applying remote changes until the tab becomes visible again, just tracking the pending revision and reconciling on visibilitychange — a solid win for multi-tab setups, with the existing conflict-reconcile path (pullAll + merge) handling any staleness if a background push happens while hidden. I'm worried some local writes might skip markDirty, which would leave lastSnapshot stale and cause the diff logic to incorrectly skip syncing a local change that differs from remote, though in that case preserving the local unsynced change is probably the safer outcome anyway.

Reading all IDB content fresh for a full local snapshot isn't the main cost — the real expense is the writes themselves plus Lix persistence and editor remounts, so I think it's fine to keep doing a full fresh read for correctness, especially since hidden tabs defer and only changed rows actually get written.

content.text:
I fixed the sync problem, and I found and merged the compact Markdown fix you were missing. Both are committed on `feat/clairic-extraction` but not pushed or deployed yet.

**Sync.** You were right that it was the cause.
- **What was wrong:** every open tab subscribed to your whole account (all manuscripts, notes and briefs). While you typed, the app pushed every 4 seconds, and each push sent the entire account back to every tab and device. Each one then rewrote every piece into local storage, re-saved its whole version-history file, and reloaded its editor, even when you'd edited a different piece.
- **What changed:** tabs now listen only for a revision number. A tab fetches your data only when it's behind and visible, and writes only what changed. The editor keeps your text, cursor and undo history unless that same piece was edited somewhere else.
- **What I measured:** I opened two tabs on the real app, using a fake server that behaves like Convex. With the old code, just two pushes sent 9.4 MB to the open tabs; with the fix, almost nothing. In both versions the tab you type in didn't reload and no typing was lost. The harness was too unreliable for a typing-speed comparison, so I don't have one.
- **Checks:** the sync tests pass, including two new checks: a tab's own push doesn't make it re-download, and a change elsewhere in your account rewrites nothing. One test failed in a combined run and passed on rerun, the same flaky interaction between test files as before.

**Fixes that hadn't landed.** I checked your other threads and branches. Only "Voice Usage Errors Before Finalization" is active, and it's on this same branch.
- Two of your fixes were committed on branches but never merged:
  - **"Render Markdown in compact and gathered notes"** (Oct 27): the compact Markdown fix.
  - **"Carry a passage connection's reason into the gathered sheet"** (Oct 27).
- Both are merged now. The one conflict was in `src/utils/markdown.ts`, and your branch's version contained everything this one had, plus an extra security fix. The Markdown and passage tests pass.
- The many `t3/*` branches are the separate native desktop port, so I didn't touch them.

**Deploying.** Production only gets these fixes when this branch goes to `main`, and it also carries everything committed last time, including the Qwik upgrade. Should I push this branch to `main` to deploy?
